findings.claim: All 60 practice questions carry another board's forms: '4 marks - Describe Two Features', '10 marks - Explain Two Reasons', '10 marks - Explain Why', '5 marks - Outline', '25 marks - Essay Using Interpretations (with SPaG)', '8 marks - Explain Causation'. Mark schemes award 'up to 5 marks' and add 'SPaG: 5 marks'. Lesson 3's exam tip coaches 'Describe Two Features' questions.
findings.truth: The thematic study is a one-hour paper of 50 marks with four questions: Describe (4), Explain (8), a second-order concept question (14) and an essay on change and/or continuity over time (24). The spec's table gives AO1 4/4/4/8 and AO2 -/4/10/16 and leaves the SPaG column empty; section 3i puts the only SPaG marks (5 each) on paper 1 question 4 and paper 3 question 2. There is no 5-, 10- or 25-mark question and no source or interpretation question.
findings.evidence: specs/ocr/history-a-J410.md - thematic-study assessment table ('The thematic study will be assessed by four questions') and section 3i; paper overview (50 marks, 1 hour written paper, no SPaG asterisk).

findings.claim: Every lesson's essay stem ends 'Use your knowledge and any interpretations you have studied', and lesson 7's mark scheme credits 'any named interpretations'.
findings.truth: No sources or interpretations are supplied in the thematic study paper. Interpretation and source work sits in the period study and the British depth study, not here.
findings.evidence: specs/ocr/history-a-J410.md - thematic-study assessment table shows AO1 and AO2 only; AO3 and AO4 columns are empty.

findings.claim: Reasonable Blackman, a Southwark silk-weaver active around 1507, who appears in London parish records
findings.truth: Reasonable Blackman was an Elizabethan silk weaver in Southwark, recorded from the 1570s to the 1590s; three of his children died in the 1592 plague. English parish registers only begin in 1538, so a 1507 parish record cannot exist. Also wrong in knowledge check 5 and flashcard 2.
findings.evidence: Miranda Kaufmann, Black Tudors (the lesson's own named source); Thomas Cromwell's 1538 injunction on parish registers.

findings.claim: operated from the Steelyard ... until Henry VIII curtailed their privileges in the 1520s
findings.truth: Henry VIII confirmed Hanseatic privileges. Edward VI's government revoked them in 1552 and Elizabeth I closed the Steelyard in 1598.
findings.evidence: Standard accounts of the Hanseatic League's London Steelyard.

findings.claim: The Match Girls Strike of 1888 at Bryant and May's factory in Whitechapel, involving many immigrant workers - placed in the lesson's Eastern European Jewish section, with the definition calling the workers 'many of them Jewish immigrants'.
findings.truth: Bryant and May's Fairfield Works stood in Bow, east London, and the matchwomen were overwhelmingly of Irish descent. The strike is not evidence of Eastern European Jewish activity. Jewish East End labour organising is better shown by the London tailors' strike of 1889. The error repeats in the conclusion, knowledge check 2, flashcard 6 and the glossary.
findings.evidence: Louise Raw, Striking a Light; Bryant and May, Fairfield Road, Bow E3.

findings.claim: William Cuffay (son of a formerly enslaved man, of Irish background in the broader movement) - credited in the mark scheme for a question about Irish migrants' contribution to British political movements.
findings.truth: Cuffay was born in Chatham to a father from St Kitts. He was not Irish and not a migrant, so he cannot answer a question about Irish migrants.
findings.evidence: Standard biographies of William Cuffay.

findings.claim: until his transportation to Australia in 1848
findings.truth: Cuffay was convicted in September 1848 and sailed for Van Diemen's Land the following year.
findings.evidence: Standard biographies of William Cuffay.

findings.claim: in Cardiff, a man named Charles Wootton drowned trying to escape a mob
findings.truth: Charles Wootton was chased into Liverpool's Queen's Dock and drowned there on 5 June 1919. The riots did also reach Cardiff, but Wootton died in Liverpool.
findings.evidence: Accounts of the 1919 Liverpool race riots.

findings.claim: The Status of Aliens Act 1914 required all foreign nationals to register with police and restricted their movement ... gave the government powers to detain or deport them.
findings.truth: Two laws passed in August 1914. The Aliens Restriction Act imposed registration, movement limits, internment and deportation. The British Nationality and Status of Aliens Act set out who counted as a British subject and how to naturalise. The lesson gives the Restriction Act's powers to the Status of Aliens Act. The spec names only 'the Status of Aliens Act 1914', so students must recognise that title. Option A: keep the spec's title but add one clause naming the Aliens Restriction Act as the registration and internment law. Option B: leave as written, because the spec's own wording is what the paper will use.
findings.evidence: specs/ocr/history-a-J410.md content bullet ('the Aliens Act 1905, the Status of Aliens Act 1914 and the British Nationality Act 1948'); Aliens Restriction Act 1914 and British Nationality and Status of Aliens Act 1914.
findings.ruling: Spec title kept; Aliens Restriction Act named in a clause.

findings.claim: the British Nationality Act, passed just weeks earlier, confirmed that all Commonwealth subjects were British citizens
findings.truth: The Windrush docked on 22 June 1948. The British Nationality Act received royal assent on 30 July 1948 and came into force on 1 January 1949, so it was passed after the ship arrived, not weeks before. The passengers travelled as British subjects under the law already in force.
findings.evidence: British Nationality Act 1948, royal assent 30 July 1948, in force 1 January 1949.

findings.claim: carrying 492 passengers from the Caribbean
findings.truth: The ship's passenger list records 1,027 passengers, of whom 802 gave a Caribbean country as their last residence. The 492 figure came from press reports counting only part of the ship.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Empire Windrush' (passenger manifest breakdown: 1,027 passengers; 802 Caribbean, 66 Polish, 119 UK, 40 elsewhere).

findings.claim: Learie Constantine ... became the first Black person appointed as a British Resident in the United Kingdom when he moved to London, and whose case became central to the 1961 Race Relations debate
findings.truth: There is no such post as 'British Resident in the United Kingdom' and there was no 1961 Race Relations debate; the first Race Relations Act was 1965. Constantine won damages from the Imperial Hotel in 1943-44, became Trinidad and Tobago's High Commissioner to the UK in 1962, and became Britain's first Black peer in 1969. The lesson's own glossary entry already says this correctly.
findings.evidence: Constantine v Imperial Hotels Ltd (1944); Race Relations Act 1965; the lesson's glossary_terms entry.

findings.claim: requiring 'patriality' (a grandparent born in Britain) to qualify for the right of abode. Around 70,000 Kenyan Asians held British passports; the 1968 Act effectively made them stateless.
findings.truth: The 1968 Act used a parent or grandparent born in the UK as a qualifying connection. The term 'patriality' and the right of abode came in with the Immigration Act 1971. Kenyan Asians kept their British passports; they lost the guarantee of entry, so they were not stateless. The 70,000 figure is not supported.
findings.evidence: Commonwealth Immigrants Act 1968; Immigration Act 1971 (right of abode, patriality).

findings.claim: Edward Heath sacked Powell from the Shadow Cabinet the same day
findings.truth: Powell spoke on 20 April 1968; Heath dismissed him on 21 April 1968. Repeated in practice question 3 and flashcard 6.
findings.evidence: Dates of the 'Rivers of Blood' speech and Powell's dismissal.

findings.claim: about 28,000 held British passports and were admitted to Britain under the 1971 Immigration Act's emergency provisions
findings.truth: The Immigration Act 1971 only came into force on 1 January 1973. The Ugandan Asians arrived in 1972 as UK passport holders and were received by the Uganda Resettlement Board, set up in August 1972.
findings.evidence: Immigration Act 1971 commencement 1 January 1973; Uganda Resettlement Board 1972.

findings.claim: The Life in the UK test, introduced in 2002 ... The test was updated in 2005 and again in 2013. (Same claim in lesson 10's content, conclusion and glossary.)
findings.truth: The Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002 provided for the test. The first tests were sat in November 2005 and the requirement was extended to settlement applicants in 2007. The handbook was rewritten in 2007 and again in 2013, so it cannot have been 'updated in 2005', the year it began.
findings.evidence: Nationality, Immigration and Asylum Act 2002; Life in the UK test launched 1 November 2005.

findings.claim: By 2007, an estimated 600,000-800,000 Polish nationals were living in Britain.
findings.truth: That range matches cumulative Worker Registration Scheme applications, not the resident population. The Poland-born population of the UK was 60,711 at the 2001 census and about 532,000 by December 2010.
findings.evidence: Wikipedia 'Foreign-born population of the United Kingdom' (60,711 in 2001; an estimated 532,000 in the year to December 2010).

findings.claim: The Scarman Report was significant in opening a sustained debate about institutional racism
findings.truth: Scarman explicitly rejected the charge that the Metropolitan Police was institutionally racist, while accepting unwitting discrimination by individual officers and social deprivation as causes. Macpherson reversed that finding in 1999. As written, the lesson blurs the very contrast it is trying to teach.
findings.evidence: Scarman Report 1981; Macpherson Report 1999.

findings.claim: the perpetrators were British-born men whose families had migrated from Pakistan
findings.truth: Three of the four 7 July 2005 bombers were British-born men of Pakistani heritage. The fourth, Germaine Lindsay, was born in Jamaica and grew up in Britain.
findings.evidence: Identities of the 7 July 2005 London bombers.

findings.claim: Violence intensified in 1190. As crusading fever swept England before the Third Crusade, anti-Jewish riots broke out in London and several other cities.
findings.truth: The London massacre took place at Richard I's coronation on 3 September 1189. The 1190 riots struck King's Lynn, Norwich, Stamford, Lincoln, Bury St Edmunds and York.
findings.evidence: Standard accounts of the 1189-90 anti-Jewish riots in England.

findings.claim: The blood libel accusations were repeatedly investigated and debunked by the authorities - Henry III at one point imprisoned the accusers of a Jewish community rather than the Jews themselves.
findings.truth: No such episode is on record and Henry III's own record runs the other way: after the death of Hugh of Lincoln in 1255 he had about 18 Jews hanged. Authorities did sometimes reject the charge - Pope Innocent IV condemned the blood libel as false in 1247 - which makes the paragraph's point without an invented English case.
findings.evidence: Little Saint Hugh of Lincoln, 1255; Innocent IV's bull of 1247 against the blood libel.

findings.claim: While Whig politicians like Lord Godolphin initially welcomed them as Protestant brethren
findings.truth: Godolphin was a Tory by background who led a ministry that had become dependent on the Whigs. The measure that drew the Palatines was the Whig general naturalisation act for foreign Protestants, passed in March 1709 and repealed in 1712.
findings.evidence: Foreign Protestants Naturalization Act 1708 (in force 1709, repealed 1712); Godolphin's party position.

findings.claim: The French Protestant Church in Soho Square, London, traces its continuous history to the refugee community of the 1680s.
findings.truth: The French Protestant Church of London was founded by charter of Edward VI in 1550, 135 years before the Huguenot influx, and moved to Soho Square in 1893.
findings.evidence: Charter of Edward VI, 1550; the Soho Square building, 1893.

findings.claim: Approximately 250,000 people in Britain have documented Huguenot ancestry. (Repeated as a creditable answer in practice question 4.)
findings.truth: No published count of 250,000 documented Huguenot descendants could be found; estimates of British Huguenot descent range from tens of thousands of documented lines to a sixth of the population, depending on method. Option A: delete the figure and keep the surnames and the church as the evidence of legacy, which is what the mark scheme really needs. Option B: keep it and source it, if Tom has a reference. Leaving an unsourced number inside a mark scheme is the worst of the three.
findings.evidence: No source found; WebSearch budget exhausted.
findings.ruling: Unsourced 250,000 figure removed from body and mark scheme.

findings.claim: Between 1672 and 1713, the Company transported an estimated 100,000 enslaved Africans - but the glossary says the same 100,000 was carried 'before its monopoly was broken in 1698'.
findings.truth: Two different windows carry the same figure, so one of them is wrong. Published estimates for the Royal African Company vary widely (roughly 100,000 to 190,000 depending on the period counted), so no single value can be asserted here.
findings.evidence: Internal inconsistency between content_html and glossary_terms.

findings.claim: Norman migrants assimilated rapidly within two or three generations, with French and English eventually merging into Middle English.
findings.truth: Norman French remained the language of law and government for roughly 300 years; English only replaced it in the courts under the Statute of Pleading of 1362. Lesson 1 of this same unit says French became the language of government and stayed there, so the two lessons contradict each other on a change-and-continuity point.
findings.evidence: Pleading in English Act 1362; lesson 1 content_html.

findings.claim: Most lesson essays sit inside a single era, for example 'How far do you agree that immigration remained the most divisive issue in British politics between 1981 and 2010?'
findings.truth: The spec says the 24-mark essay will require learners to use two of the three content sections, or all three. Single-era essay practice is useful for content recall but does not rehearse the actual question. Worth a later sweep to add cross-era stems, not an edit now.
findings.evidence: specs/ocr/history-a-J410.md - 'Question 4 will be an essay ... use information from two of the three sections of content in the specification, or all three'.

findings.claim: In 1218, Jews in England were required by royal decree to wear a distinguishing badge - a piece of yellow or white felt in the shape of the Tablets of the Law
findings.truth: The 1218 decree required a white badge. The yellow felt badge of specified size came with the Statute of Jewry in 1275. The lesson hedges with 'yellow or white', which is not wrong enough to edit but blurs a change over time.
findings.evidence: 1218 English badge decree; Statute of Jewry 1275.

summary: Every lesson carried practice labels from another board: 4/10/10/5/25/8-mark forms, an interpretations essay and 5 SPaG marks. This paper sets four questions only (Describe 4, Explain 8, second-order concept 14, essay on change and/or continuity 24; 50 marks, one hour) and carries no SPaG. Nine lessons also held content errors, the worst being the Match Girls Strike moved to Whitechapel and credited to Jewish immigrants (L6), Charles Wootton killed in Cardiff rather than Liverpool (L7), the 1948 British Nationality Act dated before the Windrush docking (L8), a garbled Learie Constantine definition (L8) and Reasonable Blackman dated to 1507 (L3). Lesson 1 was clean of content errors.
